newsitem.title: USA: Dollar drifts lower awaiting Fed chairman testimony.
newsitem.headline: Dollar drifts lower awaiting Fed chairman testimony.

text.p: The dollar drifted lower against the German mark and Japanese yen Tuesday ahead of congressional testimony by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan and the sale of five-year Treasury notes, both on Wednesday.

Greenspan is scheduled to appear before the Senate Banking Committee on Wednesday to give his semiannual testimony on the state of monetary policy and the economy. His testimony before the House Banking Committee was set for March 5.
Last December, comments by the Fed chairman about "irrational exuberance" in financial markets sent prices tumbling in many markets around the world, if only briefly.
With the Treasury also slated to sell $12.5 billion in five-year notes on Wednesday, currency traders adopted a cautious stance. Weakness in the bond market could spill over to the dollar.

"Clearly, the chairman of the Federal Reserve always has it within his powers to do damage to the U.S. financial markets," said Robert Near, vice president on the foreign exchange desk at Bank of New York. "So that's clear that the markets are concerned about him tomorrow."
The dollar fell to 1.6718 marks in late New York trading from 1.6745 marks late on Monday. The dollar fell to 121.58 Japanese yen from 122.23.
The British pound was little changed at $1.6355.
The dollar slid to Canadian $1.3598 from C$1.3620. But it rose to 1.4605 Swiss francs from 1.4580 francs.
The dollar fell against the yen in Asian trading after the Japanese government's chief spokesman, Seiroku Kajiyama, said the interest rate gap between Japan and other countries should be narrowed.

The Bank of Japan has kept official rates at low levels to try to stimulate the Japanese economy. Higher rates might strengthen the yen by making deposits denominated in that currency more attractive to investors.
Still, some traders in New York tended to play down the importance of the Kajiyama comments.
"I don't think there was much impact from his comments," said Keisuke Aso, manager of the forex service department at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi in New York.
Aso said Kajiyama's remarks were general in nature and that Kajiyama is not considered responsible for policy that effects short-term movements in the foreign exchange market.
Some traders were also locking in profits after the dollar's rapid climb in recent weeks, participants said.

"I would say, in general, the market's in a consolidative maybe even corrective phase right now from the recent moves up," said Thomas Arnold, chief foreign exchange dealer at Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank. "I think it's more that than any particular event."
Since the start of the year, the dollar has climbed against the mark and the yen, hitting a 34-month high of 1.7050 marks on Feb. 18 and a four-year high of 124.82 yen on Feb. 14.
